item.research_question: Can high pressure induce a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phase in the prototypical face-centered cubic (fcc) high-entropy alloy CrMnFeCoNi, and what are the mechanisms and retention characteristics of this transformation?
item.material_system: CrMnFeCoNi (near-equiatomic solid solution of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni)
item.processing_route: Arc-melting of equimolar constituent metals under Ar, drop casting, annealing at 1,200 °C for 24 h, powdering, and loading into a diamond anvil cell with silicone oil pressure medium and Au pressure standard; pressure increased stepwise to 54.1 GPa and decreased at ~1 GPa min⁻¹
item.test_conditions: Ambient temperature, pressures up to 54.1 GPa, angle-dispersive X-ray diffraction (λ=0.4959 Å)
key_findings: The fcc-to-hcp transformation begins at approximately 14 GPa.
The transformation is sluggish, occurring over a pressure range of >40 GPa.
The volume collapse accompanying the transformation is 0.6(4)%.
The bulk modulus of the initial fcc phase is 150(3) GPa.
The bulk modulus of the high-pressure hcp phase is 141(8) GPa.
Upon decompression from 54.1 GPa, 56(2)% of the material remains in the hcp phase at ambient pressure.
Upon decompression from 26.8 GPa, 34(1)% of the material remains in the hcp phase at ambient pressure.
Roughly 60% of the hcp volume is retained after depressurization regardless of the maximum pressure achieved.
item.mechanism: The transformation is driven by the pressure-induced suppression of local magnetic moments (primarily Fe), which destabilizes the fcc structure; the sluggish kinetics are attributed to the proportionality between pressure and the energy barrier for stacking fault formation.
item.limitations: The text notes that the hcp phase is retained due to kinetic hindrance (trapping of atoms and lattice strain) rather than thermodynamic stability, and that rapid pressure quenching might be needed to enhance retention.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that removing Fe from the alloy might enhance hcp stability and reduce the critical pressure for formation, and that high-pressure processing could be used to tailor mixtures of hard hcp and ductile fcc phases.
quotes: This martensitic transformation begins at 14 GPa and is attributed to suppression of the local magnetic moments, destabilizing the initial fcc structure.
The transformation is sluggish, occurring over a range of >40 GPa.

This pressure-induced suppression of the local magnetic moments in the initial fcc phase lessens the stabilizing effects of magnetism, such that formation of the hcp phase becomes energetically favourable by 14 GPa.
